strengths: The paper delivers a clear, impactful, and conceptually refreshing message: the dominant estimator-centric paradigm in off-policy learning (OPL) often fails in large action spaces because the optimization landscape—rather than estimation accuracy—is the primary bottleneck.

The theoretical analysis provides neat insights by deriving closed-form oracle policies for multiple estimators (cIPS, ES, MIPS, OffCEM, PC) and unifying POTEC as an optimization strategy of OffCEM rather than a distinct estimator.

The empirical evaluation is exceptionally thorough and executed on realistic, massive action spaces (MovieLens 60k, Twitch 200k, GoodReads 1M items). The controlled stress tests across batch sizes, learning rate schedules, random seeds, reward noise, and logging supports convincingly substantiate the core claims.
The paper is well-written, clearly organized, and transparent about its limitations (e.g., that PWLL is not an off-policy value estimator and cannot be used for off-policy model selection).
weaknesses: Algorithmic and theoretical originality is somewhat incremental. PWLL objectives are directly adapted from advantage/reward-weighted regression in offline RL (e.g., AWR, CRR, AWAC) and prior bandit work (LPI), while the concavity of weighted cross-entropy under linear softmax and the softmax policy gradient plateau results are essentially known (following Chen et al., 2019 and Mei et al., 2020a).

The theoretical concavity guarantees strictly hold for linear-softmax policies. Although the authors provide an intuition and remark for deep architectures, there is no formal optimization analysis when deep representations are learned end-to-end.

The semi-synthetic contextual bandit protocol (deriving contexts and rewards from user-item interactions and simulating logging policies via SVD embeddings restricted to top-k0 items) is standard in the recommendation OPL literature, but it would be beneficial to discuss the impact of logging policy misspecification and density ratio errors on PWLL relative to IPS-based approaches.

strengths: Compelling central thesis: The paper effectively challenges the prevailing 'estimator-centric' dogma in off-policy learning (OPL), convincingly showing that optimization landscape pathologies are often a much more critical bottleneck than value estimation accuracy in large action spaces.

Solid theoretical framing: The characterization of optimization plateaus scaling as O(K_eff) and exponential local maxima for linear-in-policy IPS objectives, contrasted with the concavity of policy-weighted log-likelihood (PWLL) under linear-softmax parametrizations, provides a rigorous foundation for why direct IPS maximization struggles.

Comprehensive and rigorous empirical stress tests: The evaluation spans realistic large-scale recommendation benchmarks with up to 1M actions (MovieLens, Twitch, GoodReads) under varied batch sizes, learning rate schedules, seeds, reward noise, and support sizes. The empirical evidence consistently supports the claims.

Practical utility and clear actionable guidance: The paper derives two actionable design principles—objective-aware policy parametrization (aligning policy support/factorization with estimator oracle policies) and adopting PWLL objectives for policy learning—that yield substantial practical gains without added complexity.

Honest discussion of scope and limitations: The authors explicitly clarify that PWLL is not an off-policy value estimator (and therefore cannot be used for policy evaluation or model selection) and candidly discuss the loss of strict concavity in deep end-to-end architectures.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: The proposed PWLL objectives (LPI, cLPI, RegKL) are adaptations or specializations of existing concepts (e.g., Liang & Vlassis 2022, reward-weighted regression, and offline RL behavioral cloning updates). While the authors acknowledge this positioning transparently, the algorithmic toolkit itself is largely familiar.

Theoretical proofs are largely adaptations of existing work: Propositions 2.1 and 2.2 rely directly on proofs and techniques from Mei et al. (2020a) and Chen et al. (2019) for the single-context setting, representing straightforward extensions rather than new theoretical machinery.

Semi-synthetic bandit setup: The experiments rely on standard offline collaborative filtering datasets converted to bandit feedback via synthetic SVD-based logging policies and top-k truncations. While standard in academic literature, evaluating on datasets with real counterfactual production logs would further strengthen the empirical claims.

strengths: Compelling conceptual reframing: The paper makes a persuasive and timely argument shifting the focus in large-action off-policy learning (OPL) from estimator variance reduction (OPE fidelity) to optimization landscape geometry and trainability.

Insightful analysis of oracle policies and objective-aware parametrization: Deriving closed-form oracle policies for various estimators (cIPS, ES, DR, MIPS, OffCEM, PC) provides clear intuition on their implicit biases and naturally justifies restricting the effective action space (e.g., support restriction or cluster-level factorization like POTEC). Reinterpreting POTEC as an optimization parameterization of OffCEM rather than a fundamentally distinct estimator is particularly illuminating.

Theoretical clarity: Formalizing the concavity (and strong concavity under l2 regularization) of policy-weighted log-likelihood (PWLL) objectives under linear-softmax parameterizations (Proposition 3.1) and connecting it to stochastic optimization convergence rates (Propositions D.4 and D.5) clearly highlights why cross-entropy/log-likelihood formulations avoid the vanishing gradient and plateau issues of linear-in-pi objectives.

Extensive large-scale empirical evaluation: The empirical study covers three realistic recommendation benchmarks with extreme action spaces (MovieLens with 60k, Twitch with 200k, and GoodReads with 1M actions). The evaluation is rigorous, demonstrating consistent gains across multiple learning rate schedules, batch sizes, random seeds, noise levels, and support sizes.

Transparent discussion of positioning and limitations: The authors explicitly clarify that PWLL is not a novel algorithmic contribution of their own (citing connections to AWR, CRR, and LPI) and clearly outline limitations regarding deep network parameterizations and coverage dependencies.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: As acknowledged by the authors, PWLL objectives are direct contextual-bandit equivalents of reward-weighted regression / local policy improvement / advantage-weighted behavioral cloning long known in offline reinforcement learning and recommender systems.

Worst-case nature of theoretical optimization pathologies: Propositions 2.1 and 2.2 are adapted from existing literature (Mei et al., 2020a; Chen et al., 2019) and establish the existence of pathological instances where gradient ascent is trapped on plateaus or encounters exponentially many local maxima, but they do not prove that standard bandit instances necessarily exhibit these extremes.

Concavity guarantee restricted to linear heads: The formal optimization advantages of PWLL strictly apply to linear-softmax models (or fixed-backbone settings). While cross-entropy gradients empirically remain better-behaved than policy gradients in deep models, formal concavity and global convergence guarantees are lost when training representations end-to-end.

Dependence on logging policy support: Both objective-aware support restriction (Claim 2.3) and PWLL objectives restrict policy improvement to the actions supported by the logging policy, meaning these methods cannot discover high-reward actions outside the logging support without auxiliary reward modeling or smoothing.
